doc.title: Dave Pell interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996

chapter: Lester Young and the Prez Conference
title: Playing in odd keys: Ray Brown and Lester Young
summary: Pell explains three flats, tells of Ray Brown's E-blues trap, and says Lester Young deliberately changed keys to unsettle horn players.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: You know since we are on camera, can you explain this to our students? [hand gesture]

It’s in three flats because down is flats and if you are going to play in four sharps, like Lester, or seven sharps like Lester, he always did that kind of number, so you’d figure in all the sharps and then flat the fifth. And there’s a story about Ray Brown. We were doing a show one day and they were playing the blues, we were not even paying attention. And they’re playing the blues, while the cameras are being set up, the bands always used to do films you know and things like that. And Ray Brown is playing the blues and they’re cooking, boy. And he said, “okay, Dave, let’s go.” And I get up and play and I realized all of a sudden they’re playing in E, which puts you in an F sharp on your horn, and I says holy mackerel, what are you doing? And I fumbled and fumbled through a couple of choruses and sat down, and Ray Brown looks at me and says, “I told you you are a twelve handicap saxophone player.” Because we play golf together all the time. But see Lester did that, Lester Young. If everybody was playing “Lady Be Good” in F or G, he would play it in G, and then all the horn players had to play in A. And that’s very tough to play on certain horns. Or in E, which is great for guitar, but terrible for the © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
horns to play in. And Lester did that on purpose. Half the time he played “Lady Be Good”, no, no, “let’s play it up a tone,” and oh, everybody else around him died.
They’re falling out and he’s exciting, right?
He doesn’t think sharps and flats, he hears it and plays it. He doesn’t care. He didn’t care. But it was very interesting. A lot of guys did that, out of meanness you know.
